title: Variable Star — Algebra I, Level 1 knowledge graph
subject: Algebra I

conventions.id: Stable kebab-case identifier. Never renamed once shipped; it is the `kpId` in learn:* signals.
conventions.prerequisites: Direct prerequisites only. The relation is a DAG and is transitively reduced: if a -> b -> c then c never lists a. Proved by review/p03/kg-validate.mjs.
conventions.difficulty: 1-5 band. Selects the learner-model parameter row in `model.bands` and the item difficulty centre on the logit scale.
conventions.estMinutes: Scored-item time only, for a median learner: acquisition + first retention check. Excludes traversal, narrative and review of this node inside later nodes.
conventions.misconceptions[].diagnosticSignature: A predicate the item bank (P17) must be able to evaluate from item parameters and the learner's response. `item:` names the generated form with its parameters; `response ==` gives the value or structure a learner holding this misconception produces. Four hard rules, all linted by review/p03/kg-validate.mjs. (1) SEPARABLE: no two misconceptions on the same node may share a signature, or the wrong-answer feedback cannot tell them apart and L7 is unachievable on that node. (2) DISCRIMINATING: a generated item is only valid for a misconception if the signature produces a value different from the correct answer. (3) CONSTRUCTED: the signature must be evaluable from a response the learner BUILDS — a value, an expression, a placement, a partition, a counterexample. It must never be phrased as a yes/no or a pick-one, because the item bank will faithfully serve what is written here, and a yes/no item has a blind-success rate of 0.50, which model.formScorability excludes from the scored path entirely. (4) PAIRWISE-SEPARATED: on a GENERATED INSTANCE, no two misconceptions on the same node may evaluate to the same response. Rule (1) separates the signatures as STRINGS and rule (2) separates each signature from the CORRECT answer; neither notices that a particular choice of parameters can collapse two different wrong ideas onto one number, and when that happens the wrong-answer feedback in section 6.2 of design/learning-architecture.md attributes the error to whichever misconception is listed first and stages the wrong collapse, which is L7 failing silently on an item that passed every other check. This is a constraint on the GENERATOR, not on the wording: P17 must evaluate all of a node's signatures on each candidate stem before serving it and reject the stem if any two agree. It is cheap — the signatures are closed-form — and the cost is measured rather than assumed: review/p03/signature-collide.mjs exhaustively scans the declared parameter space of the eight node families whose signatures share a stem and can be evaluated in closed form, and prints the share of otherwise-valid stems the rule rejects: eq-combine-side 8.75% of 11384, eq-distribute 7.02% of 1054, eq-one-add 5.56% of 324, eq-both-sides 3.38% of 13128, eq-two-step 1.46% of 820, distribute-numeric 1.45% of 3716, distribute-variable 0.00% of 2375, eq-one-mult 0.00% of 55. A rejection rate above 25% on any family is a build failure, because at that point the misconceptions are not distinguishable and the node needs different ones rather than a filter. That threshold has already earned itself: the first run of this scan flagged eq-distribute at 100%, because `divide-bracket-only` (response r - q) and the round-3 `distribute-onto-both-sides` (response (p*r - p*q)/p) are the same expression for every p, so the node shipped two misconceptions that no item could ever tell apart. It was replaced by `coefficient-never-undone` (response r - p*q), which is a real error and a separable one.
conventions.standards: Keys into content/standards.json. Every node carries at least one.
conventions.worldHook: The physical act in the world that IS this knowledge point. Not a quiz framing. Nouns are provisional until design/world.md lands; the verbs are the contract.
conventions.localization: Every learner-facing string in this file is EN source text for a locale key, not the string that ships. Key shape: kp.<id>.title, kp.<id>.short, kp.<id>.description, kp.<id>.hook, misconception.<id>.description. P20 owns content/locales. ES and PL must localise the mathematics, not only the words: decimal comma, the ES/PL ordering of 'less than' phrases (which is the whole point of translate-order and cannot be translated literally), locale-appropriate variable letters, and the ES/PL convention of writing multiplication with a centre dot rather than a cross.

model.note: Single machine-readable source of truth for the numbers argued in design/learning-architecture.md. P16 reads this; it does not hard-code duplicates.

bkt.formsEligibleForMasteryNote: M2 and M3 count ONLY opportunities served in these forms. This is the field the gate reads; it is not advice. A form outside this list may not increment scored, atBand or the form set, and may not trigger a BKT update (see model.forms.scored). Derived, not decreed: see model.trueGuessByForm and the derivation in review/p03/kg-validate.mjs, which recomputes the eligible set from the identifiability caps on every run and fails if it disagrees with this array.
bkt.phasesEligibleForMasteryNote: The second axis of the same gate, and it is read exactly the way formsEligibleForMastery is read: an opportunity may increment `scored`, `atBand` or the form set ONLY IF its form is in formsEligibleForMastery AND its teaching phase is in this array. M2's six opportunities and M3's two distinct forms therefore cannot be filled from a scaffolded item, however that item is priced. This is a separate field from model.phases.scored on purpose, and the difference is the whole point: `guided-1` IS scorable (it moves P(known), at a phase-aware guess that is honest about the scaffold) but it is NOT mastery-eligible, because a first step someone else placed is evidence about the rest of the item, not an independent demonstration of the knowledge point. Derived, not decreed: review/p03/kg-validate.mjs recomputes the scorable (form x phase) matrix from the identifiability caps on every run and fails if the phase axis disagrees with model.phases.scored, or if this array admits a phase whose true blind rate exceeds the solo baseline.

identifiabilityCaps.note: These caps are a REJECTION test on an item's PRICE, never a clamp on an observed rate, and the price has two factors: the form (how big the answer space is) and the teaching phase (how much of it the world has already filled in). Clamping is the bug this field exists to forbid: an engine that clamps a yes/no item's true blind-success rate of 0.50 down to maxGuess 0.30 credits every lucky coin flip with more evidence than it is worth, and the mastery gate leaks. The same arithmetic applies to help: an item answered after a hint surface has appeared has a true blind rate of 0.85, and pricing it at the form's 0.03 is the identical error committed on the other axis. If a form's or a phase's trueGuess exceeds maxTrueGuess, or trueGuess + maxSlip reaches maxSlipPlusGuess, that form or phase is not scorable at all — the engine must refuse the BKT update, not soften it.

guessByForm.note: MODEL BELIEF. Multiplier on the band's `guess` parameter, giving the guess the BKT update uses for a form. This is what the engine thinks blind success is worth. It is not evidence of anything on its own — compare it against trueGuessByForm below.

trueGuessByForm.note: GROUND TRUTH. The probability a responder with zero knowledge of the knowledge point produces a correct response in this form, derived from the size of the form's answer space — not from any model parameter. review/p03/mastery-sim.mjs draws bot responses from THESE numbers, never from guessByForm, so the simulation can measure the gate instead of restating it. If P17 ships a form whose real answer space is smaller than assumed here, this table is the thing that must change first.

derivation.construct: A numeric slot accepts the integers in [-20, 20] plus fraction forms: 1/41 = 0.024. Expression-valued slots are far larger. 0.03 is the conservative ceiling over both.
derivation.repair: One of about six joints in a shown build is wrong; the error site is not signposted, so a blind responder must both find it and correct it. Rounded up to match construct rather than argued lower.
derivation.generate: Produce a case with a named property. Many answers are correct, but none is reachable by luck, because the property has to be checked. 0.02.

guessByPhase.note: MODEL BELIEF, second axis. Multiplier on the band's `guess`, exactly parallel to guessByForm, giving what the engine thinks blind success is worth once the WORLD has already done part of the item. Composed with guessByForm by max, never by product: modelledGuess(band, form, phase) = band.guess x max(guessByForm[form], guessByPhase[phase]). Max is the right composition because a scaffold puts a FLOOR under blind success — placing the first step cannot make an item harder to fluke — and because a product would let the generate multiplier (x0.6) undercut the scaffold floor and reintroduce the exact under-pricing this table exists to remove.

derivation.solo: No help. The form's own multiplier stands alone; the phase contributes nothing.
derivation.guided-1: The smallest round multiplier that is conservative against a true 0.08 at EVERY band. Band 1 needs at least 0.08 / 0.05 = 1.6; band 5 must stay under maxGuess, 0.30 / 0.10 = 3.0. The window [1.6, 3.0] is non-empty, so guided-1 is repairable and 2.0 sits inside it: modelled 0.100 / 0.120 / 0.140 / 0.160 / 0.200 against a true 0.08.
derivation.guided-2: Recorded, not used. 0.17 / 0.05 = 3.4 is what conservatism needs at band 1, and 3.0 is the most maxGuess allows at band 5. The window is EMPTY, so no multiplier makes guided-2 scorable — the same structural failure as select4.
derivation.guided-3: Recorded, not used. 0.85 / 0.05 = 17.0, which is 0.17 modelled at band 1 and 1.70 at band 5, both far past maxGuess 0.30. Unreachable, like judge2.

trueGuessByPhase.note: GROUND TRUTH, second axis. The probability a responder with zero knowledge of the knowledge point produces a correct response WHEN THE WORLD HAS ALREADY DONE THIS MUCH OF THE ITEM, derived from what the scaffold removes from the answer space — not from any model parameter. Composed with trueGuessByForm by max: trueGuess(form, phase) = max(trueGuessByForm[form], trueGuessByPhase[phase]). A scaffold can only shrink the answer space, so the phase floor dominates whenever it is higher. review/p03/mastery-sim.mjs draws bot responses from THESE numbers. If P18 ships a scaffold that gives away more than assumed here — a hint that names the answer rather than the next move, a constraint that leaves two seatable parts rather than six — this table is the first thing that has to change, and section 5.0 has to be re-run.

derivation.solo: No scaffold, no hint surface, no pre-placement. 0.00 contributed by the phase; the form's own rate is the whole rate.
derivation.guided-1: The first step is already placed, so the remaining answer space is the tail of the item — roughly one in twelve of the completions that will physically seat. 0.08, rounded up from 1/12 = 0.083 being the near miss it is.
derivation.guided-2: The answer space is constrained to legal moves: about six parts will seat and the rest fall off. 1/6 = 0.167 -> 0.17. This is not a small number and it is not a rounding error; it is a four-option multiple choice wearing a workshop.
derivation.guided-3: A hint surface naming the next move appears after antiGuessing.hintSurfaceMs of no input. Reading it and doing what it says is the intended behaviour and it usually works — that is what makes it a good hint and what makes it worthless as evidence. 0.85.
derivation.model: The world has just performed the identical act in front of the learner and only the last move is missing. Copying what you watched thirty seconds ago is most of the item. 0.70.

formScorability.note: Which forms may enter the scored path, and why. This block is a DERIVATION, recomputed by review/p03/kg-validate.mjs from bands + guessByForm + trueGuessByForm + identifiabilityCaps on every run; the validator fails if the recomputation disagrees with model.forms.scored or model.bkt.formsEligibleForMastery. A form is scorable iff, for EVERY band: (a) trueGuess <= maxTrueGuess; (b) trueGuess + maxSlip < maxSlipPlusGuess; (c) conservatism — the modelled guess (band.guess x guessByForm) is at least trueGuess, so a correct answer never moves P(known) further than the truth warrants; (d) the modelled guess itself satisfies maxGuess and maxSlipPlusGuess without being clamped. NOTE that the four rules are run again, unchanged, over the PHASE axis in phaseScorability and over the composed (form x phase) matrix in pairScorability: a rule that ejects select4 for being a one-in-four and then prices a six-seatable-parts scaffold at one-in-thirty-three is not a rule, it is a preference.

construct.reason: 0.03 true against 0.05-0.10 modelled: the model under-credits luck at every band, which is the safe direction.

generate.reason: 0.02 true against 0.030-0.060 modelled after the x0.6 multiplier. Conservative at every band.

select4.reason: Fails (c) at bands 1-3: modelled 0.170 / 0.204 / 0.238 against a true 0.25, so every lucky quarter-chance is credited as knowledge. And no repair is possible: making it conservative at band 1 needs a multiplier of at least 5.0 (0.05 x 5.0 = 0.25), while staying under maxGuess at band 5 needs at most 3.0 (0.10 x 3.0 = 0.30). 5.0 > 3.0, so NO multiplier makes select4 scorable across all five bands. It is excluded structurally, not by preference.

judge2.reason: Fails (a): true 0.50 > maxTrueGuess 0.30. Fails (b): 0.50 + 0.16 = 0.66, past maxSlipPlusGuess 0.5, so BKT is not identifiable. Fails (d): no multiplier can reach a modelled 0.50 while respecting maxGuess 0.30. A yes/no item is excluded from the scored path entirely — it is not merely discouraged.

phaseScorability.note: The same four rules as formScorability, run over the TEACHING PHASE instead of the form, because scaffolding shrinks an answer space exactly the way a multiple choice does. Recomputed by review/p03/kg-validate.mjs from bands + guessByPhase + trueGuessByPhase + identifiabilityCaps on every run; the validator fails if the recomputation disagrees with model.phases.scored or model.bkt.phasesEligibleForMastery. Rules, verbatim from formScorability: (a) trueGuess <= maxTrueGuess; (b) trueGuess + maxSlip < maxSlipPlusGuess; (c) conservatism — the modelled guess (band.guess x guessByPhase) is at least trueGuess; (d) the modelled guess itself satisfies maxGuess and maxSlipPlusGuess without being clamped.

solo.reason: Contributes 0.00 to the blind rate. The composed price is the form's price, which is what formScorability already cleared.

guided-1.reason: 0.08 true against 0.100-0.200 modelled once guessByPhase['guided-1'] = 2.0 is applied. Passes (a) 0.08 <= 0.30, (b) 0.08 + 0.16 = 0.24 < 0.50, (c) at every band, (d) 0.200 <= 0.30 and 0.200 + 0.16 = 0.36 < 0.50. Scorable — but see model.bkt.phasesEligibleForMastery: scorable is not mastery-eligible. At the round-3 price (band.guess x guessByForm alone, 0.050 / 0.060 / 0.070 / 0.080 / 0.100 for construct) it FAILED (c) at bands 1-3, which is the defect this block exists to fix. It is the only one of the four scaffolded phases that is repairable at all, because 0.08 / 0.05 = 1.6 leaves the window [1.6, 3.0] non-empty.

guided-2.reason: Two failures, and the second is the one that closes the door. (i) Under the ROUND-3 price — the form's multiplier alone, no phase term — it fails (c) at every band: modelled 0.050 / 0.060 / 0.070 / 0.080 / 0.100 against a true 0.17, so five times out of six a part that will not seat is refused by the world and the sixth is credited to the learner as knowledge. (ii) Under the most favourable price available, guessByPhase 3.4 (the smallest multiplier that is conservative at band 1), it fails (d) at band 5: modelled 0.340 > maxGuess 0.30, and 0.340 + slip 0.16 = 0.50, which is exactly maxSlipPlusGuess and therefore outside it. Conservatism at band 1 needs at least 3.4 while maxGuess at band 5 permits at most 3.0, and 3.4 > 3.0, so NO multiplier makes guided-2 scorable across all five bands. This is the select4 argument with different numerals and it has the same ending: excluded structurally, not by preference.

guided-3.reason: Fails (a): true 0.85 > maxTrueGuess 0.30. Fails (b): 0.85 + 0.16 = 1.01, far past maxSlipPlusGuess 0.50, so BKT is not identifiable at all. Fails (d): no multiplier can reach a modelled 0.85 while respecting maxGuess 0.30. This is judge2's failure exactly, and it is worse than judge2 by a wide margin: a coin is 0.50 and a hint that names the next move is 0.85. An item answered after the hint surface has appeared is excluded from the scored path entirely.

model.reason: Fails (a), (b) and (d) at 0.70 true, for the same reason guided-3 does. Already excluded by design — section 6.1 has always said the model phase is a demonstration and not evidence — but it is derived here rather than asserted, so the exclusion survives an engineer who reads only the JSON.

pairScorability.note: The composed matrix, which is the thing P16 actually implements. An item's price has two factors and both must clear the four rules: trueGuess(form, phase) = max(trueGuessByForm[form], trueGuessByPhase[phase]) and modelledGuess(band, form, phase) = band.guess x max(guessByForm[form], guessByPhase[phase]). review/p03/kg-validate.mjs evaluates all 25 cells of forms x phases on every run and asserts the scorable set is exactly the product listed below; the file fails the build if a single cell disagrees.
pairScorability.scorablePairs: forms {construct, repair, generate} x phases {solo, guided-1} — 6 of 25 cells
pairScorability.masteryEligiblePairs: forms {construct, repair, generate} x phases {solo} — 3 of 25 cells. M2 and M3 count these and nothing else.
pairScorability.worstComposedPrice: band 5, generate, guided-1: true 0.08 against modelled 0.10 x ... = 0.200. Conservative by 2.5x. The tightest cell is band 1, construct, guided-1: true 0.08 against modelled 0.100, conservative by 1.25x, which is the cell that sets guessByPhase['guided-1'] >= 1.6.

forms.cycleIndexNote: The acquisition form is order[scoredCount % order.length], where scoredCount is the node's CUMULATIVE count of MASTERY-ELIGIBLE scored opportunities so far — the same counter M2 reads, so it advances on solo items only — evaluated BEFORE the current response is scored. The cycle is never restarted at `construct` when P crosses cycleAbove; it is a running index into a fixed list. This is load-bearing arithmetic, not a style note: restarting the cycle serves `construct` (guess x1.0) where the running index serves `generate` (guess x0.6), which changes the posterior. Tying it to the M2 counter rather than to raw attempts also means the form cycle cannot be advanced by grinding scaffolded items. review/p03/kp-trace.mjs and review/p03/mastery-sim.mjs both index on scoredCount.
forms.unscoredPolicy: An unscored form produces NO BKT update, NO M2 or M3 credit, no prerequisite credit and no theta movement. It is legal in exactly two places: inside a `model` phase, where the world is demonstrating and the learner is confirming what they just watched, and in narrative surfaces that are not learning opportunities. P17 must not generate a scored item in an unscored form; P16 must refuse to score one if it arrives anyway. learn:respond still fires so P18/P24 can react, with scored:false.
forms.itemBankRule: Every diagnosticSignature in this file is written so it can be evaluated from a CONSTRUCTED response. If a signature ever reads as a yes/no or pick-one question, the item bank will serve it as judge2 or select4 and the gate leaks. review/p03/kg-validate.mjs lints for that shape and fails the build.

phases.fadeNote: fadeOrder is listed from MOST help to LEAST help and the direction words are banned from this design because they were ambiguous in round 3. A correct response ADVANCES one position along fadeOrder (less help next time); advancing past the last position promotes to `solo`. An error RETREATS one position (more help next time); retreating before the first position enters `model`, subject to modelEventsPerNodePerSession, and stays at guided-1 once that budget is spent. There is also a shortcut, and it is the one that keeps the acquisition path short for a learner who does not need it: P(known) >= soloThreshold with the previous response on this node correct promotes to `solo` from anywhere in the ladder.
phases.hintedNote: `hinted` mirrors the flag that already exists on spacing.consolidation, spacing.retentionCheck and spacing.review, and it means the same thing in all five places: the world put information on the screen that the learner did not produce. guided-1 and guided-2 are false because a placed first step and a constrained answer space are not information surfaces — they shrink the answer space, which is what trueGuessByPhase prices, and they are refused scoring on that basis rather than on this flag. guided-3 and model are true. P16 must set `hinted` on learn:respond from what the world ACTUALLY DID on that item, not from the phase name, because P18 may surface help for an accessibility reason in a phase whose default is false, and antiGuessing.hintedCorrectPolicy has to fire on the real event.
phases.unscoredPolicyNote: Inert means inert in BOTH directions — no posterior movement up or down, no M2/M3 credit, no prerequisite credit, no theta movement — exactly like an unscored form. learn:respond still fires, with scored:false, so P18/P24 can react. The symmetry is the point, and it draws a line this design needs: WHO CHOSE THE HELP. When the DIRECTOR scaffolds, the item stops being a measurement of the learner and becomes a measurement of the learner-plus-scaffold, which is not the quantity P(known) is about; the honest response is to record nothing and let the fade ladder, not the posterior, decide what comes next. Punishing a learner for failing an item the world had already half-done would be the opposite error, and an earlier draft of this round did exactly that: it cost the median simulated learner 34 percentage points of Level 1 mastery, because a learner who needs a scaffold spends most of their guided items wrong and their posterior could then only ever fall. When the LEARNER chooses the help — idling past antiGuessing.hintSurfaceMs on an item that was otherwise scorable — the asymmetric rule applies instead: antiGuessing.hintedCorrectPolicy is not-scored-upward and hintedWrongPolicy is scored-normally, because there the item WAS a measurement and the help only inflates the correct side of it.
phases.dominantStrategyNote: This block plus antiGuessing.hintedCorrectPolicy is the answer to the only strategy a real fifteen-year-old actually runs: idle until the hint surfaces, read it, type what it says, repeat. Under the round-3 rules that strategy was strictly dominant — it raised P(known) at 0.85 true success against a 0.03-0.10 modelled guess, and it filled M2's six opportunities and M3's two forms. Under these rules it buys nothing at all and its 15% error rate still costs, so idling is now strictly dominated by trying. review/p03/mastery-sim.mjs runs it as a cohort and as an isolated-gate arm, with the round-3 rules kept alive beside it as a control so the size of the closed leak is a measured number rather than a claim.

modelPhase: first encounter with the node AND P(known) < modelPhaseThreshold
band centre - 0.6 > theta + ability.modelPhaseTriggerGap (even the easiest variant is out of reach) AND P(known) < modelPhaseThreshold
two consecutive errors on this node matching the SAME misconception id
the node has lapsed twice inside 7 days AND P(known) < lapseReentry.unlessBelow
a retreat off the front of fadeOrder
guidedEntry: immediately after a model event, at fadeOrder[0]
P(known) < soloThreshold on the first item of a visit
retreatAfterConsecutiveErrors consecutive errors on this node (retreat one position along fadeOrder)
soloEntry: P(known) >= soloThreshold AND the previous response on this node was correct
advancing past the last position of fadeOrder
always, unconditionally, for consolidation, retentionCheck and review

phases.triggersNote: Two conditions here are tighter than the round-3 prose and both were measured, not preferred. (1) The easiest-variant-out-of-reach trigger now carries `AND P(known) < modelPhaseThreshold`. Without it the trigger reads only the GLOBAL ability estimate, so a learner who is doing fine on a band-5 node gets re-lectured on it every session merely because their theta is still low; in simulation that fired 1.7 model events per node and burned 9% of the session budget on demonstrations nobody needed. (2) retreatAfterConsecutiveErrors is 2, not 1. A single wrong answer is what the `slip` parameter is FOR — 8% to 16% of responses from a learner who genuinely holds the skill are wrong — and scaffolding a slip is both insulting and expensive.
phases.secondsPerItemByPhaseNote: The session budget is TIME, not item count, and a scaffolded item does not cost what an unscaffolded one costs. A `model` event is a demonstration you watch and one move you make: about 12 s of world plus 10 s of hand. guided-1 hands you the first step, so it is the tail of the work. guided-2 is a full construction in which illegal parts will not seat, which removes the dead ends rather than the work. guided-3 and solo are full items at the 46 s that design/learning-architecture.md section 5 budgets everywhere else; the 12 s a hint-abuser spends idling comes out of that same 46 s, which is part of why idling is expensive rather than free. Consolidation, retention and review are always solo and always 46 s.
phases.lapseReentryNote: Round 3 said two contradictory things about this and an implementer had to pick one: section 3 rule 5 said two lapses inside 7 days re-enter at `guided`, not `model`, while section 6.1's trigger list said two lapses inside 7 days AND P(known) < 0.30 trigger `model`. Both intents are right and the resolution is the `unlessBelow` field: re-enter at guided-1, because you do not re-lecture an adult about a sign error, UNLESS the posterior has fallen below 0.30, at which point the knowledge really has gone and a demonstration is the honest response.

spacing.consolidationNote: passAtLeast is 0 on purpose and it is written down rather than left implicit. Consolidation is a PRACTICE PASS, not a second gate: its two items are scored normally, so getting them wrong pushes P(known) down and can strand the node below masteryThreshold at the retention check — but the transition provisional -> awaiting-retention is not itself conditional on how many of the two were right. The gate that certifies is retentionCheck, and it carries both passAtLeast and requiresThresholdAtCheck. An engineer implementing section 2 must not invent a pass requirement here; the anti-guessing numbers in section 5.0 were measured against exactly this shape.
spacing.retentionCheckNote: requiresThresholdAtCheck means M4 is a conjunction, not a count: the node certifies only if at least passAtLeast of items are correct AND P(known) is still >= bkt.masteryThreshold after all four have been scored. Both halves matter. The count alone would let a learner who slipped on the fourth item certify off a posterior that had already fallen through the threshold; the posterior alone would let 2-of-4 through on a favourable prior. review/p03/mastery-sim.mjs enforces the conjunction, and the per-node guessing bounds in design/learning-architecture.md section 5.0 were measured against it.
spacing.formsNote: consolidation, retentionCheck and review all draw forms from model.bkt.formsEligibleForMastery and all run at phase `solo` with hinted false. Stated three times on purpose, on both axes: these are the three surfaces where an engineer following a checklist is most likely to reach for a quick yes/no confirmation or to leave the hint timer running, and those are exactly the two surfaces a guesser would farm.
spacing.relearnNote: Savings — relearning being faster than learning — is a property of re-acquiring something you ONCE HELD. A failed first retention check is not a lapse of knowledge; it is a failed first certification, and it earns the ordinary learn rate. Handing the boost to a learner who has never been certified is not generosity, it is a hole: the learn rate sets a FLOOR under the all-wrong BKT fixed point, so a higher learn rate means a responder who is never right still drifts upward. At the round-1 cap of 0.45 the band-1 relearn floor was 0.489, and from there a SINGLE lucky answer reached 0.9704 and cleared M1 on its own. The cap is now 0.32, chosen as the largest round value at which no band, in either state, lets one lucky answer clear the threshold — review/p03/kg-validate.mjs asserts that invariant on every run.

antiGuessing.hintedPolicyNote: The exact counterpart of the latency floor, on the other end of the clock, and it exists because without it the floor makes IDLING strictly dominant: answering fast and right is penalised, answering slow and right after reading the hint is not. `hinted` is a per-response fact — did the world put information on the screen before this response was committed — and P16 reads it off the event, not off the phase name (see phases.hintedNote). Any response flagged hinted is not scored upward and does not count toward M2 or M3, in ANY phase, including solo: if P18 surfaces help in solo for an accessibility reason, that item stops being evidence, which is the correct trade. hintSurfaceMs is 12000 and is the same 12 s the guided-3 scaffold uses; it is stated here as well so the anti-gaming rule and the teaching rule can never drift apart.
antiGuessing.notScoredUpwardDefinition: One rule, two triggers, and both are things the LEARNER chose: a correct response committed under the latency floor, and a correct response committed after the learner idled past hintSurfaceMs and read the help. Such a response produces no posterior update, no scored/atBand/form increment, no prerequisite credit and no theta gain; a WRONG response in the same circumstances is scored normally, at the item's ordinary guess. Speed cannot help you, help cannot help you, and both can still hurt you. This is NOT the rule for a scaffold the director chose — see model.phases.unscoredPolicy, which is `inert` in both directions, because a learner must never be punished for being taught.

nodes.title: A letter can hold a number
nodes.description: A variable is a name for a quantity that is unknown or that varies. The same letter means the same value everywhere in one expression; two different letters may still hold the same value.

misconceptions.description: Reads the letter as an abbreviation for an object rather than a number, and so reverses a comparison (the classic students-and-professors reversal).
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'there are k times as many A as B, relate a and b' -> response == 'k·a = b' instead of 'a = k·b'

misconceptions.description: Believes different letters must stand for different numbers, so never produces a pair in which they coincide.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: charge two cores x and y so that x + y == 2·v and x − y == 0 (unique solution x = y = v) -> response supplies x ≠ y, or leaves the second core empty

misconceptions.description: Believes a letter carries a fixed value from its position in the alphabet (a = 1, b = 2), so ignores the value supplied.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate letter L at value v -> response == alphabetIndex(L)

nodes.standardsNote: FL.MA.6.AR.1.1 was tagged here in round 3 and is dropped. It reads 'translate written descriptions into algebraic expressions and translate algebraic expressions into written descriptions'; this node translates nothing — it is about what a letter is. The code stays on translate-phrase, translate-order and translate-sentence, which are the three nodes that actually do that act. Florida, like TEKS, has no student expectation about what a variable IS, so this node is a named Florida hole.
nodes.worldHook: Grip an empty resonance core and it stays dark until you shove a numeric charge into it — the core is the letter, the charge is whatever you decide it holds.

nodes.title: Order of operations with numbers
nodes.description: Grouping first, then exponents, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right. Multiplication is not privileged over division, nor addition over subtraction.

misconceptions.description: Evaluates strictly left to right, ignoring precedence entirely.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a + b·c -> response == (a + b)·c

misconceptions.description: Treats multiplication as always preceding division rather than sharing a rank left to right.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a ÷ b · c -> response == a ÷ (b·c)

misconceptions.description: Treats addition as always preceding subtraction rather than sharing a rank left to right.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a − b + c -> response == a − (b + c)

nodes.standardsNote: FL.MA.6.AR.1.3 was tagged here in round 3 and is dropped. It reads 'evaluate algebraic expressions using substitution and order of operations'; this node has no letters in it, so there is no algebraic expression and nothing is substituted. It stays tagged on eval-substitute, eval-signed and eval-formula, where both halves of the code are true. Florida files purely numeric order of operations outside the Algebraic Reasoning strand this graph maps to, so this node is a named Florida hole.
nodes.worldHook: Feed a chain of charges into a smelter whose intake ports fire in a fixed sequence; open the wrong port first and what pours out is slag you have to carry.

nodes.title: Terms, coefficients, constants, factors
nodes.description: Cut an expression at its plus and minus signs and the pieces that come away are its terms. Inside a term the number multiplying the variable is the coefficient; a term with no variable is a constant; the sign in front belongs to the term that follows it.

misconceptions.description: Splits a term at a multiplication sign, counting the coefficient and the variable as separate terms.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'how many terms in a·x + b' -> response == 3

misconceptions.description: Says x has no coefficient rather than coefficient 1, and −x no coefficient rather than −1.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'coefficient of x in x + b' -> response ∈ {0, 'none'}

misconceptions.description: Detaches the minus sign from the term it belongs to, so a − b·x is read as terms a and b·x.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'second term of a − b·x' -> response == 'b·x' (sign dropped)

nodes.worldHook: Snap a glowing expression rail apart at its plus and minus joints; whatever comes away in one piece is a term, and the number stamped on its collar is the coefficient.

nodes.title: What binds to what once a letter is in the way
nodes.description: Precedence inside an algebraic expression: 2x² means 2·(x·x), −x² is not (−x)², juxtaposition means multiply, and a bracket groups before it multiplies.

misconceptions.description: Reads a·x² as (a·x)², letting the exponent capture the coefficient.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate a·x² at x = v -> response == (a·v)²

misconceptions.description: Reads −x² as (−x)², so the result comes out positive.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate −x² at x = v -> response == +v²

misconceptions.description: Reads a·x written as ax as though it meant a + x.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate a·x at x = v -> response == a + v

nodes.worldHook: Hold a reader lens over a live expression and its groupings light up in the order the machine will actually consume them, one bracket at a time.

nodes.title: Put the number in and see what comes out
nodes.description: Replace every occurrence of the variable with its value, then evaluate the resulting numerical expression in order.

misconceptions.description: Replaces only the leftmost occurrence of a variable that appears more than once.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate x² + x at x = v -> response == v² + x-left-unreplaced, i.e. the value obtained when only the leftmost occurrence is substituted

misconceptions.description: Writes the value beside the rest of the expression instead of substituting into it.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate a + n at n = v -> response == concat(a, v)

misconceptions.description: Substitutes correctly but loses the coefficient's multiplication.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate a·x at x = v -> response == v

nodes.worldHook: Slam a numeric charge into every socket a letter left open, then let the machine run and read the output dial with your own eyes.

nodes.title: Substituting negatives without losing the sign
nodes.description: A substituted negative arrives inside its own parentheses: (−3)² is 9 but −3² is −9, and subtracting a negative adds.

misconceptions.description: Substitutes −v without parentheses, so x² becomes −v².
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate x² at x = −v -> response == −(v²)

misconceptions.description: Reads a − (−b) as a − b, dropping one negative instead of cancelling both.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate a − x at x = −b -> response == a − b

misconceptions.description: Applies the product rule for signs to a sum, so (−a) + (−b) comes out positive.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate x + y at x = −a, y = −b -> response == a + b

nodes.worldHook: Charge a core with an inverted, cold charge and watch the machine bracket it for you before it lets it into the pipeline — then try to do it yourself without the bracket.

nodes.title: Running a formula with more than one letter
nodes.description: Evaluate expressions and real formulas in two or more variables by sending each value to its own letter, not to whichever socket is nearest.

misconceptions.description: Assigns values in the order they were given rather than by the letters they are named for.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate a − b at a = p, b = q -> response == q − p

misconceptions.description: Uses a single value in every socket, treating all letters as the same unknown.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate a + b at a = p, b = q -> response ∈ {2p, 2q}

misconceptions.description: Evaluates only the part containing the first variable and reports that.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: evaluate c·a + d·b -> response == c·p

nodes.worldHook: A machine with two intake ports demands two different charges; feed the same one into both and it jams loudly enough that the whole ridge hears it.

nodes.title: Turning words into an expression
nodes.description: Map sum, difference, product, quotient, increased by, twice and per onto the operations, and name the unknown with a letter you choose on purpose.

misconceptions.description: Applies a keyword rule without reading the sentence's structure, so grouping is lost.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'a groups of n, and b more' -> response == a + n + b

misconceptions.description: Produces a purely numeric expression, leaving the unknown out entirely.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any phrase containing an unnamed quantity -> response contains no variable symbol

misconceptions.description: Reads 'twice a number' as adding two rather than multiplying by two.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'twice n' -> response == n + 2

nodes.worldHook: A voice over the comms names a quantity out loud and you have to have the matching rail welded before the transmission finishes.

nodes.title: Phrases that refuse to commute
nodes.description: 'Five less than n' is n − 5 and 'n divided into 20' is 20 ÷ n. When the operation does not commute, the words and the symbols run in opposite directions.

misconceptions.description: Writes 'a less than n' in the order the words arrive.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'a less than n' -> response == a − n

misconceptions.description: Writes 'n divided into a' with the dividend and divisor swapped.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'n divided into a' -> response == n ÷ a

misconceptions.description: Writes 'subtract n from a' in the order the words arrive.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'subtract n from a' -> response == n − a

nodes.worldHook: Two rails that look identical seat in opposite directions; put one in backwards and the current runs the wrong way down the span and you feel it in the deck.

nodes.title: Licences to rearrange
nodes.description: Addition and multiplication may be reordered and regrouped; subtraction and division may not. Adding zero and multiplying by one change nothing, and that is what makes them useful.

misconceptions.description: Reorders a subtraction as though it commuted.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: rewrite a − b as an equivalent expression whose first term is b -> response == b − a (correct: −b + a)

misconceptions.description: Regroups across a subtraction sign, so a − (b + c) becomes (a − b) + c.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a − (b + c) -> response == (a − b) + c

misconceptions.description: Uses zero as the multiplicative identity or one as the additive identity.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: simplify x·0 or x + 1 -> response == x

nodes.worldHook: Some couplings on a rail spin freely and some are keyed to one orientation; the only way to learn which is to put your hands on them and try to turn them.

nodes.title: Which pieces are the same kind of thing
nodes.description: Terms are like when they carry the same variable raised to the same power. 3x and 5x are like; 3x and 5x², and 3x and 5y, and 3x and 5, are not.

misconceptions.description: Treats every term containing a letter as like every other, so 3x and 2y are sorted into one group.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: sort the 5 terms of a·x + b·y + c + d·x + e·y into weld groups (correct partition {a·x, d·x}{b·y, e·y}{c}) -> response places all four variable terms in one group

misconceptions.description: Treats a constant as like a variable term and welds it onto the variable group.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: sort the 5 terms of a·x + b + c·x + d·y + e into weld groups (correct partition {a·x, c·x}{d·y}{b, e}) -> response places b or e in a group containing a variable term

misconceptions.description: Matches on the letter alone and ignores the exponent.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: sort the 5 terms of a·x + b·x² + c·x + d·x² + e into weld groups (correct partition {a·x, c·x}{b·x², d·x²}{e}) -> response places an x² term in the same group as an x term

nodes.worldHook: A cut span leaves five beams scattered on the deck. Drag them into weld stacks by profile and pull the lever: stacks of one profile fuse, a stack with a stranger in it throws sparks and drops the lot.

nodes.title: Adding the same kind of thing
nodes.description: Add or subtract the coefficients of like terms and leave the variable part exactly as it was, carrying each term's sign with it.

misconceptions.description: Combines unlike terms by fusing their variable parts.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b·y -> response == (a + b)·x·y

misconceptions.description: Adds the variable parts as well as the coefficients, raising the power.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b·x -> response == (a + b)·x²

misconceptions.description: Moves a term to sit beside its partner but leaves its minus sign where it was.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x − c − b·x -> response == (a − b)·x + c

nodes.worldHook: Weld matching beams end to end. The weld shortens the stack you are carrying but it never changes the profile of what you carry.

nodes.title: One factor across a whole group
nodes.description: a(b + c) = ab + ac, seen as one rectangle split into two pieces. The factor outside touches every term inside, not just the first.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies only the first term inside the bracket and copies the rest.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a(b + c) -> response == a·b + c

misconceptions.description: Distributes across multiplication as though it were addition.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a(b·c) -> response == (a·b)·(a·c)

misconceptions.description: Adds the outside factor to each term instead of multiplying.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a(b + c) -> response == (a + b) + (a + c)

nodes.worldHook: Pour one charge into a splitter and it has to reach every branch. Cap a branch to save charge and the whole manifold ruptures in your face.

nodes.title: Distributing over a group with a letter in it
nodes.description: a(bx + c) = abx + ac. The coefficient multiplies the coefficient; the variable rides along untouched.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies the variable along with its coefficient, raising the power.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a(b·x + c) -> response == (a·b)·x² + a·c

misconceptions.description: Reaches the variable term and leaves the constant inside untouched.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a(b·x + c) -> response == (a·b)·x + c

misconceptions.description: Adds the outside factor to each coefficient instead of multiplying.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a(b·x + c) -> response == (a + b)·x + (a + c)

nodes.worldHook: The splitter now feeds a live rail. The charge scales the rail's rating without changing what the rail is made of, and you can watch the rating climb.

nodes.title: Distributing a minus sign
nodes.description: −(x − 5) = −x + 5, and a − b(x + c) subtracts the whole product. When the factor outside is negative every term inside flips — all of them.

misconceptions.description: Flips the sign of the first term inside and leaves the rest alone.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: −(b·x + c) -> response == −b·x + c

misconceptions.description: Drops the leading minus entirely when opening the bracket.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: −(b·x + c) -> response == b·x + c

misconceptions.description: Subtracts the outside numbers first and then distributes the result.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a − b(x + c) -> response == (a − b)·x + (a − b)·c

nodes.worldHook: An inverted charge run through the splitter flips the polarity of every branch at once. Miss one branch and the manifold shorts across the whole span.

nodes.title: Open every group, then gather
nodes.description: The standard pipeline: clear grouping symbols by distributing, then combine like terms, then check by substituting one value into both the original and the result.

misconceptions.description: Combines a term outside a bracket with the factor in front of it before distributing.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a + b(x + c) -> response == (a + b)·x + (a + b)·c

misconceptions.description: Distributes correctly but leaves two like terms uncombined.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any -> response is equivalent to the item but still contains two like terms

misconceptions.description: Fuses the surviving variable term and constant into a single term.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any whose simplest form is m·x + n -> response == (m + n)·x

nodes.worldHook: Run a tangled span through the press: it opens every bracket, welds every match, and spits out the shortest rail that still crosses the gap.

nodes.title: Two builds, one machine
nodes.description: Two expressions are equivalent when they agree for every substitution. One disagreeing value disproves it; a chain of legal rewrites proves it.

misconceptions.description: Concludes equivalence from a single agreeing substitution, usually 0 or 1, and stops looking.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: supply a value of x at which E₁ and E₂ differ, for a pair that agrees at x ∈ {0, 1} and differs at every |x| ≥ 2 -> response ∈ {0, 1}, or the learner welds the pair identical without ever entering a value with |x| ≥ 2

misconceptions.description: Concludes non-equivalence from surface form alone without rewriting, so hunts for a separating value that does not exist.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: complete the partly-built E₂ so it agrees with E₁ at every value, where the stem of E₂ is already an equivalent rewrite of E₁ in a different surface form -> response rebuilds the stem into E₁'s surface form and thereby breaks it, or submits a candidate x* with E₁(x*) == E₂(x*) as a separator

misconceptions.description: Has already produced a disagreeing substitution and still welds the pair identical.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any pair -> response welds the pair identical while the learner's own substitution record on this item already contains an x* with E₁(x*) ≠ E₂(x*)

nodes.worldHook: Two spans of different shape sit on the same test rig. Dial in a load yourself and watch for the one that snaps first — or, if you are sure nothing separates them, weld them into a single stamped part and stake your rig on it.

nodes.title: An equation is a claim you can test
nodes.description: An equation claims two expressions have the same value. A solution is a number that makes the claim true, and substituting is how you find out.

misconceptions.description: Reads = as an instruction to compute rather than an assertion of sameness, and chains a running total across it.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any -> response contains a chained equality such as a + b = c = d where c ≠ d

misconceptions.description: Reports a value without substituting it back, and reports one that fails.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any -> substituting the response into the item's equation yields a false statement

misconceptions.description: Believes an equation containing a letter is true for every number, so any charge to hand will do.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: from a magazine of six distinct charges, exactly one of which satisfies x + a = b, load every charge that locks the bridge (the response is a subset, 64 possible) -> response == all six charges

nodes.worldHook: Two spans reach out over a chasm and meet, or do not. Drop a charge in and the bridge either locks solid or lets it fall into the dark.

nodes.title: Whatever you do to one side
nodes.description: Adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing both sides by the same value keeps the claim true — never dividing by zero. That is the only licence behind every step you will ever take.

misconceptions.description: Applies an operation to one side and leaves the other untouched.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any equation -> response equation differs from the item by an operation applied to exactly one side

misconceptions.description: Adds on one side and subtracts on the other, mistaking 'balance' for 'opposite'.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any equation -> response equation applies mutually inverse operations to the two sides

misconceptions.description: Divides both sides by an expression that can be zero, typically one containing the unknown.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any equation -> response step divides both sides by an expression containing the unknown

nodes.standardsNote: TEKS.A.5A and FL.MA.912.AR.2.1 were tagged here in round 3 and are dropped. TEKS.A.5A is 'solve linear equations in one variable, including those for which the application of the distributive property is necessary and for which variables are included on both sides'; this node distributes nothing, has no variable on the second side, and does not solve. FL.MA.912.AR.2.1 is 'given a real-world context, write and solve one-variable multi-step linear equations'; this node has no context and solves nothing. Both were the nearest adjacent code, which is the padding section 7 of design/learning-architecture.md refuses to do. Neither TEKS nor Florida legislates the properties of equality as a standalone expectation, so this node is a named hole in both, not a mapping failure.
nodes.worldHook: The bridge is a real balance. Lift a mass off your span and the far span rises until you lift exactly the same mass off it too.

nodes.title: Undoing a plus or a minus
nodes.description: Solve x + p = q and x − p = q by applying the inverse operation to both sides, then check the number against the original claim.

misconceptions.description: Repeats the operation shown instead of inverting it.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: x + p = q -> response == q + p

misconceptions.description: Computes p − q instead of q − p.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: x + p = q -> response == p − q

misconceptions.description: Treats x − p = q as though the inverse were subtraction.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: x − p = q -> response == q − p

nodes.worldHook: Pull the surplus ballast off your span. The deck only stays level if you pull exactly the same ballast off the far span in the same motion.

nodes.title: Undoing a times or a divide
nodes.description: Solve ax = b and x ÷ a = b by dividing or multiplying both sides by a, reading a coefficient as the multiplication it is.

misconceptions.description: Subtracts the coefficient instead of dividing by it.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x = b -> response == b − a

misconceptions.description: Computes a ÷ b instead of b ÷ a.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x = b -> response == a / b

misconceptions.description: Divides where the equation calls for multiplying.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: x / a = b -> response == b / a

nodes.worldHook: A span built from five identical segments has to be cut into five before you can weigh one. Cut the wrong span and the bridge drops.

nodes.title: Two moves, in the right order
nodes.description: For ax + b = c, undo the addition first and the multiplication second — the reverse of the order that built the expression. c − b is routinely negative even when the solution is a clean integer, so signed arithmetic is load-bearing here rather than incidental.

misconceptions.description: Divides by the coefficient while the constant is still attached, and divides only part of the side.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b = c -> response == (c / a) − b

misconceptions.description: Undoes the addition and then multiplies instead of dividing.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b = c -> response == (c − b)·a

misconceptions.description: Adds the constant to the other side instead of subtracting it.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b = c -> response == (c + b) / a

nodes.worldHook: The span is bolted and then ballasted. You have to unballast before you can unbolt, and the bridge tells you instantly if you reach for the bolts first.

nodes.title: Tidy one side before you move anything
nodes.description: When one side carries several like terms, combine them first so what remains is a two-step equation you already own.

misconceptions.description: Combines the constant on the left with the number on the right as though the equals sign were a plus, so nothing gets inverted on the way across.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b·x + c = d -> response == (d + c) / (a + b)

misconceptions.description: Starts inverse operations before combining and loses one of the like terms.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b·x + c = d -> response == (d − c) / a

misconceptions.description: Combines the constant into the coefficient of the variable term.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b·x + c = d -> response == d / (a + b + c)

nodes.worldHook: Weld the duplicate beams on your side before you start unloading. The crane physically will not lift two separate stacks at once.

nodes.title: Open the bracket, or divide it away
nodes.description: p(x + q) = r yields to distributing first or to dividing both sides by p first. Both are legal; one is usually far less work, and choosing is part of the skill.

misconceptions.description: Distributes to the variable only and leaves the constant inside untouched.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: p(x + q) = r -> response == (r − q) / p

misconceptions.description: Divides the bracketed side by p and leaves the other side as it was.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: p(x + q) = r -> response == r − q

misconceptions.description: Opens the bracket correctly and clears the constant, then stops — the coefficient is treated as already dealt with because it has been written out.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: p(x + q) = r -> response == r − p·q

nodes.worldHook: A sealed module spans the gap. You can crack it open into its parts or shrink the entire bridge by its factor — both land you on the same footing, and one takes half as long.

nodes.title: Getting the unknown onto one side
nodes.description: Subtract the smaller variable term from both sides so the unknown appears once, then finish it as the two-step equation it has become.

misconceptions.description: Moves a variable term across the equals sign without changing its sign.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b = c·x + d -> response == (d − b) / (a + c)

misconceptions.description: Removes the variable term from one side without removing it from the other.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b = c·x + d -> response == (d − b) / a

misconceptions.description: Collects the constants onto the side that still carries the unknown.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b = c·x + d -> response == (d + b) / (a − c)

nodes.worldHook: Both spans carry unknown cores. Strip the same number off each until only one side still holds any, and the bridge finally reads out a number.

nodes.title: When there is no answer, and when every number is
nodes.description: Keep transforming until you reach x = a (one solution), a = a (every number works) or a = b with a ≠ b (nothing works), and say what that means out loud.

misconceptions.description: Reports x = 0 whenever the variable terms cancel.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: an identity or contradiction -> response == 0

misconceptions.description: Calls an identity 'no solution' because the variable disappeared.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: reduces to a = a -> response == 'no solution'

misconceptions.description: Produces a number for an equation that reduces to a false statement.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: reduces to a = b with a ≠ b -> response is a number

nodes.worldHook: Some gaps take exactly one footing, some accept any footing you bring, and some cannot be bridged at all. The chasm tells you which by what it does to your test charge.

nodes.title: Turning a sentence into an equation
nodes.description: A sentence with 'is', 'equals', 'the same as' or 'gives' becomes an equation: name the unknown, build each side, join them with =.

misconceptions.description: Builds one side only and never asserts the equality.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a sentence asserting equality -> response contains no '='

misconceptions.description: Puts the whole sentence on one side and something else on the other, ignoring where the claim splits.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: 'b more than a times n is c' -> response == b + a·n + c

misconceptions.description: Writes a correctly shaped equation whose letter names a different quantity from the one the question asks about.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any -> response equation is well formed but its declared meaning for the letter contradicts the question asked

nodes.worldHook: Speak a claim into a balance gate and it materialises as two unfinished spans that you now have to build until they meet.

nodes.title: Build the equation the situation is already making
nodes.description: Name the unknown, write each side from the story, solve, then check the number against the story and not merely against the equation.

misconceptions.description: Reaches a number by informal arithmetic and has nothing to fall back on when the situation puts the unknown on both sides.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a comparison context -> response contains no equation and is wrong on the both-sides variant while right on the one-step variant

misconceptions.description: Solves correctly but reports x when the story asked for a quantity derived from x.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any whose question asks for f(x) -> response == x

misconceptions.description: Accepts a solution the context forbids, such as a negative count or a fractional person.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any with a declared domain constraint -> response violates that constraint

nodes.worldHook: The chasm has no printed span length. You read it off the terrain, build both sides from what the world tells you, and walk across your own answer.

nodes.title: A claim with room in it
nodes.description: The symbols <, >, ≤ and ≥ assert an order rather than an equality. The solution is a set of numbers, drawn as a ray with an open or a filled end.

misconceptions.description: Reports one number as the solution of an inequality.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any inequality -> response is a single value where a set is required

misconceptions.description: Uses a filled endpoint for a strict symbol or an open endpoint for an inclusive one.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any -> response graph endpoint style contradicts the strictness of the symbol

misconceptions.description: Reads c < x as 'x is less than c' because the smaller-looking end is on the left.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: c < x -> response shades the ray below c

nodes.worldHook: A gate that admits everything past a threshold: you set the mark with your hands and the world lights up the entire stretch of charges that will get through.

nodes.title: Solving with the order still intact
nodes.description: Adding or subtracting the same amount, or multiplying or dividing by a positive number, leaves the direction of the inequality exactly where it was.

misconceptions.description: Reverses the symbol after an addition or subtraction step.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: x + p < q -> response == x > q − p

misconceptions.description: Finds the boundary value and stops, giving no direction at all.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any inequality -> response == boundary value with no relational symbol

misconceptions.description: Reverses because a negative number is present anywhere, not because of the sign of a multiplier.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: x + (−p) < q -> response reverses the symbol

nodes.worldHook: Raise both gates by the same amount and the admitted stretch slides along the rail but never turns around.

nodes.title: The one move that turns the gate around
nodes.description: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality symbol. Nothing else does, and this is the whole reason inequalities are not equations.

misconceptions.description: Divides by a negative coefficient and keeps the direction.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: (−a)·x < b -> response == x < b / (−a)

misconceptions.description: Reverses the symbol correctly but reports a positive quotient.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: (−a)·x < b -> response == x > b / a

misconceptions.description: Reverses after subtracting a negative, treating any sign change as a flip trigger.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: x − (−p) > q -> response reverses the symbol

nodes.worldHook: Invert the gate's charge and the whole admitted stretch snaps to the other side of the mark. You feel it flip through the handle before you see it.

nodes.title: Two moves and a direction to protect
nodes.description: Solve px + q > r the way you solve px + q = r, watching for the single step that can reverse the symbol, and then read the answer back into the situation that produced it.

misconceptions.description: Reverses the symbol at both steps, ending up where it started.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: (−a)·x + b > c -> response keeps the original direction after two reversals

misconceptions.description: Divides only the constant on the far side by the coefficient.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: a·x + b > c -> response == x > c − b

misconceptions.description: Reports a strict inequality where the situation requires an inclusive one, or the reverse.
misconceptions.diagnosticSignature: item: any with a declared inclusivity constraint -> response strictness contradicts that constraint

nodes.worldHook: A gate with both a ratchet and a threshold: unratchet, unthreshold, and if you inverted anything on the way, the admitted stretch is on the other side of the mark when you look up.
